claim: Other heroes' ordeals feel lesser because the event is not dwelt on and leaves no lingering change; Hobb dwells and lets it change the character.
source: A Dribble of Ink interview (Aidan Moher, 2007)
quote: the event is not dwelt on

verdict.trueWording: they seem lesser because the event is not dwelt on
verdict.note: Quote exact and the first half is fully supported: 'many fantasy tales where the heroes or heroines endure some truly awful experiences, but they seem lesser because the event is not dwelt on, and in some cases, it doesn't seem to have lingering effects or change the character in any way.' Two gaps: (a) the page hedges 'in some cases' where the claim asserts flatly that such events leave no lingering change; (b) the page nowhere says Hobb dwells on the event - the nearest wording is 'the character experiences them deeply and thus the reader feels those events more strongly.' 'Lets it change the character' is supported by the adjacent baggage paragraph; the dwelling limb is inference.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: that Hobb herself dwells on the event - the page says only that her characters experience events deeply

claim: The Hobb name was created to write with a depth of feeling she did not usually indulge.
quote: a depth of feeling that I didn't usually indulge

verdict.trueWording: With the new name she wrote with that depth of feeling
verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'was created to' — the page gives the depth of feeling as what she then wrote, not as the stated reason the Hobb name was adopted
verdict.note: gizmodo.com HTTP 200; the page reproduces the full Inheritance preface, so the source attribution is right. Quote exact: 'I wrote with a depth of feeling that I didn't usually indulge.' But the page's stated purposes for the name change are breaking with the past, the appeal of a 'secret identity', and an agreed 'opportunity for me to break out of my "Megan Lindholm" voice and tell a big compelling story in a very lively way'. The depth of feeling is the sentence that follows as consequence. Restate as effect, not purpose.

feature: every character main character of own story
claim: Each character, villain included, is written as the main character in his own story.
quote: the main character in his own story

verdict.trueWording: let each character be the main character in his own story
verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'villain included' — the word villain does not occur anywhere on this page (0 occurrences); its examples are a walk-on barmaid and minor characters written to take a bullet or be the romantic prize
verdict.note: Quote is an exact substring of 'My technique with characters is to try to let each character be the main character in his own story.' The villain limb is real but belongs to a different source — the OF Blog 2003 interview (index 19's page): 'even the villain is wondering what is for dinner tonight... If you put on the villain's skin, you have to love him or at least understand him.' Either drop the villain limb here or cite OF Blog for it.

claim: How a character reacts to an event reveals more than exposition does.

verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'more than exposition does' — the page makes no comparison to exposition; the word exposition never appears, and no ranking of reaction against telling is stated
verdict.note: Quote exact, but it occurs only in the transcript's editorial key-points header ('Reaction shots reveal character!'), not in anyone's speech. Hobb's own version is unranked: 'how the person reacts to that is a great way to build character... all of the secondary, the reaction shots of this happens, how did my character react?' The claim's comparative is an addition; state it as 'reaction reveals character' without the versus-exposition ranking.

feature: food constrained by technology, geography, climate
claim: A meal must be believable for the technology level, geography and climate, and such details fall naturally into the tale.
source: Fran Wilde, Cooking the Books guest post (2014)
quote: the technology level, the geography and climate

verdict.trueWording: The meal has to be believable in terms of the technology level, the geography and climate, and the transportation available.
verdict.note: Quote verbatim, and the believability limb is exact. But the page says meal detail 'takes a bit of thought and sometimes the pitfalls are not obvious'; the 'naturally fall into place in a tale' line sits in a different answer and refers to status-marking details (below/above the salt, dress, sleeping quarters), not to technology/geography/climate.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: that such technology, geography and climate details 'fall naturally into the tale'

claim: Her writing log records researching diseases of sheep and inserting chapter headings as bridge scaffolding.

verdict.trueWording: But that doesn't reflect that I ... inserting chapter headings for bridge work I need to create, researched diseases of sheep (it's relevant!)
verdict.note: robinhobb.com/blog/posts/41755 fetched HTTP 200; post is 'How to Write a Book When You Don't Have Time to Write', article:published_time 2022-11-03, so the November 2022 attribution holds. Quote 'researched diseases of sheep' is verbatim, and the chapter-headings-for-bridge-work limb is verbatim. What the page does NOT support is the framing: the log records start/stop times and word count ('Keep a writing log. Jot down when you start, how many words/pages you have at the beginning of your session, and then log when you stop writing'), and the sheep research and chapter headings are introduced precisely as what the day's 585-word count 'doesn't reflect' -- they are outside the log, not recorded in it.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: that the writing log records these tasks -- the post presents them as what the log's word count does NOT reflect

claim: Character is shown through inventories of the mundane on the mantel and the desk.
source: The Huntress and the Wolf (Substack essay)
quote: medicinal unguents on the mantel, two pens at the ready

verdict.trueWording: cataloged the medicinal unguents on the mantel, the two pens at the ready
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the desk - the page names no desk anywhere (grep for "desk" returns zero hits); the catalogue is the mantel, the two pens, and "the Stones puzzle on the table"
verdict.note: Also note the supplied quote is not word-for-word: the page reads "the two pens at the ready" (definite article dropped in the claim). The mantel/inventory-as-characterisation core is supported - Fitz cataloguing Lant's room as evidence of training that "is still running beneath the surface constantly and automatically".

claim: A sympathetic critic finds overreliance on adverbs stunts the Liveship novels' flow.
quote: overreliance on adverbs often stunts the novel's flow

verdict.trueWording: Her overreliance on adverbs often stunts the novel's flow
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the plural "the Liveship novels'" - the page says "the novel's flow" (singular), inside its Ship of Magic discussion; it makes no such charge against The Mad Ship or Ship of Destiny
verdict.note: Quotation verbatim. "Sympathetic critic" is supported: the piece (Lew Kelly, Fantasy-Faction, 19 Aug 2014) opens "Credit goes to Robin Hobb for doing something new and challenging" and calls the trilogy "wonderfully plotted with plenty of deeply created characters".

feature: loss as what is not received
claim: Loss is rendered through what Fitz does not get, and compressed with 'After a time'.
source: Jeffrey David Outcalt, Substack close reading
quote: no princess saved, no true love

verdict.trueWording: There is no princess saved, no true love. The hero is not lauded by the realm and given riches
verdict.unsupportedLimb: compressed with 'After a time' - the essay never discusses that phrase as a device; "After a time" occurs exactly once on the page, inside a block quotation of Hobb's novel (Starling's kiss), with no analytic comment on it
verdict.note: The loss-as-absence limb is supported verbatim. Jeffrey O, "Lies Are What A Man Needs Most", 20 Jan 2025.

claim: Elliott notes that Hobb introduces the ruined city Kelsingra through what Fitz fails to perceive there.
source: Geoffrey B. Elliott, 'Sites of Memory in Robin Hobb's Realm of the Elderlings' (ICMS 2021)
quote: he finds it empty, perceiving no signs of life around him

verdict.unsupportedLimb: that Elliott presents this as how Hobb *introduces* Kelsingra, i.e. through Fitz's non-perception
verdict.trueWording: "When FitzChivalry first encounters Kelsingra, he finds it empty"
verdict.note: The quotation is on the page word for word: "When FitzChivalry first encounters Kelsingra, he finds it empty, perceiving no signs of life around him;". But Elliott makes no claim about Hobb's technique of introduction, and the same sentence continues into positive perception, not absence: "as he searches it, he finds that 'Whole domes of roofs had fallen in...outer walls had fallen away entirely' ... and sees, among others, 'the tatters of ancient hangings, a collapsed wooden bench.'" Elliott also introduces Kelsingra two sentences earlier in his own descriptive voice ('That city is itself a silent memorial of a bygone civilization'), and later notes the city 'replays' its memories to Fitz, 'immersing him in images of the daily lives of inhabitants' -- so the city is not rendered through what Fitz fails to perceive. Grade is PARTIAL, not VERIFIED: the narrative-craft limb is the claim's gloss, not Elliott's.

claim: Garnes takes Hobb's coinage 'nitterdy-natterdy' as an English lexical resource for intensification in her contrastive corpus.
source: Inmaculada Garnes, 'Analisis pragmatico contrastivo ingles/espanol de la intensificacion verbal en textos literarios', Estudios de Traduccion 6 (2016) 39-53
routeHint: open-access PDF at revistas.ucm.es (found via OpenAlex); the article is in Spanish and a running header splits the sentence around this phrase

verdict.unsupportedLimb: that 'nitterdy-natterdy' is Hobb's coinage - the article only cites the phrase as occurring in her novel, never says she invented it
verdict.trueWording: English uses the expression nitterdy-natterdy, from Hobb's Assassin's Apprentice
verdict.note: Estudios de Traduccion PDF fetched from revistas.ucm.es and extracted (15 pp.); article confirmed as Garnes, Estud. trad. 2016, 6: 39-53. Section 5.3 'Otros recursos lexicos', printed p. 47: example (9a) is quoted from Assassin's Apprentice and "En ingles se utiliza la expresion nitterdy-natterdy." Quote exact, and the section's framing ("otras expresiones que contienen la nocion semantica de iteracion o duracion de la accion y una evaluacion negativa") supports 'English lexical resource for intensification'. Only the word 'coinage' is unsourced.

claim: Page says Hobb serves up characterisation only when it is immediately significant to a choice or tactic.
source: M Harold Page, novelist, Black Gate craft dissection of Fool's Assassin, 2016
quote: Hobb always serves up characterisation when it is immediately significant

verdict.trueWording: Hobb always serves up characterisation when it is immediately significant to choices or tactics
verdict.note: Quote is verbatim, but the page says 'always ... when', not 'only ... when' — the converse. Page reserves the restrictive 'only' for description in the very next bullet ('She only delivers description when it's part of a conflict'), so the contrast is deliberate and the claim's 'only' is not on the page.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the restrictive 'only' — the page asserts 'always serves up characterisation when it is immediately significant', which does not exclude characterisation at other moments
